candidates.title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
candidates.content: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence

candidates.title: SearchHorizonBench: A Benchmark for Search Value in AI Agents
candidates.content: AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. candidates.title: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents
candidates.content: Generative models increasingly expose a reasoning effort setting that lets users scale inference-time compute, trading higher cost for potentially improved performance. Users must choose an effort level before knowing whether extra reasoning will help, and even a successful run does not reveal whether the effort purchased was necessary. Reasoning effort is therefore a credence good: buyers observe the outcome but cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for. In this work, we measure the counterfactual effect of effort levels on both proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, spanning single-call reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. Effort, it turns out, does not consistently preserve tasks that lower effort solves, can overspend, and can change trajectory behavior. First, we find that although higher effort can raise accuracy in aggregate, it frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved. Second, on the subset of easy tasks that every effort level solves, higher effort is generally more costly, with the highest effort level costing up to 42x as much as the lowest. candidates.title: Asymptomatic Carotid Revascularization May Be Justified, but Not to Improve Cognition
candidates.content: Stroke is a feared complication of atherosclerotic carotid artery stenosis. After years of debate regarding the value of revascularizing asymptomatic carotid stenosis in the modern era of intensive medical prevention with antiplatelet therapy and high-intensity statins, the CREST-2 trial revisited this question in a pair of randomized clinical trials: one trial comparing carotid endarterectomy plus best medical management vs medical therapy alone and the other comparing carotid artery stenting plus best medical management vs medial therapy alone. The topline findings showed that carotid artery stenting, but not carotid endarterectomy, significantly reduced the risk of the primary outcome of a composite of stroke or death within 44 days or ipsilateral stroke within up to 4 years compared with medical therapy alone among patients without contralateral stenosis who were good procedural candidates.

candidates.title: Errors in Confidence Intervals

These confidence intervals have been corrected in the Abstract, Results section of the text, Figure 2, Figure 3, Table 2, and Supplement 3. None of the corrected confidence intervals change the statistical interpretation of the results, no point estimates or P values are affected, and the overall conclusions of the study are unchanged. The accompanying Editorial has also been updated to reflect the changes. These articles were corrected online.

candidates.title: Microsatellite expansion redirects chromatin modifiers to confer insect resistance to Bt bioinsecticides
candidates.content: Abstract Microsatellites are highly mutable genomic elements, yet their role in adaptive gene regulation in insects remains poorly understood. Here, we show that a tetranucleotide (ATGT) microsatellite expansion in the promoter of ABCC2 , a key Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) toxin receptor gene, epigenetically silences its expression and confers resistance to Bt Cry1Ac toxin in Plutella xylostella (L.). Mechanistically, long repeats (≥27 units) in Cry1Ac-resistant strains preferentially recruit the histone methyltransferase E(z), promoting H3K27me2/3 deposition, chromatin compaction, and transcriptional silencing, whereas short repeats in susceptible strains maintain open chromatin through Tip60-mediated H4K5 acetylation. This repeat expansion alone is sufficient to repress ABCC2 , thereby conferring Bt resistance, while repeat length, chromatin state, and associated phenotypes partially revert under relaxed selection. candidates.title: Uracil overload triggers global genome instability and dUTPdysgenesis
candidates.content: Abstract Uracil accumulation in DNA is a pervasive threat to genomic integrity, yet the global dynamics of how uracil overload drives genome instability remain elusive. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains with attenuated dUTPase ( DUT1 ) expression, we mapped the landscapes of genomic alterations including point mutations, recombination, and aneuploidy. Deletion of the UNG1 suppressed most induced mutations and loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH), identifying base excision repair as the primary driver of genomic alterations, whereas aneuploidy directly depends on the persistence of intact genomic uracil. Mechanistically, beyond localized bypass of static AP sites by translesion synthesis polymerases, the massive influx of uracil lesions induces a repair bottleneck by depleting Ung1 and Apn1. This resource titration, coupled with downstream processing intermediates, primarily drives mutagenesis at heterologous nonthymine positions. Furthermore, persistent static AP sites preferentially stimulate homologous recombination sub-pathway that yield interstitial LOH, whereas Apn1-mediated processing channels recombination toward terminal LOH. candidates.title: Genetic control couples TGFβ-independent pluripotent stem cell renewal to deterministic forward programming across germ layers
candidates.content: Reproducible and scalable manufacture of human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) derivatives requires control over expansion and differentiation. Transcription factor-mediated forward programming can place hiPSC differentiation under genetic control, but expansion still relies on extracellular growth-factor supplementation, increasing process complexity and operator dependence. Here we introduce GERALT (Genetically Enhanced Renewal and Autonomous Lineage Transdifferentiation), a push-pull genetic circuit assembled through targeted safe-harbour integration that couples NANOG-supported, TGF{beta}-independent renewal to doxycycline-inducible lineage programming and simultaneous NANOG silencing. GERALT maintained pluripotency during extended TGF{beta} withdrawal in both adherent and suspension culture, yet remained programmable towards myogenic, neuronal, and hepatic fates. Compared with the established OPTi-OX platform in myogenesis, GERALT enabled differentiation in simplified medium while canalising and accelerating commitment. candidates.title: DAPE-PD: Diffusion adaptation of genomic foundation model enables tailored-generation of cis-regulatory DNA
candidates.content: Genomic foundation models (GFMs) have transformed our ability to learn the evolutionary language encoded in genomes, yet their potential for programmable regulatory DNA engineering remains underexplored. Regulatory function depends on combinatorial interactions among distributed sequence elements, motivating generation with bidirectional context. Here, we introduce DAPE-PD (Diffusion Adaptation of Pretrained Evo for Promoter Design), which adapts the autoregressive Evo model into a bidirectional masked diffusion model without foundation-scale retraining. DAPE-PD combines pretrained genomic representations with iterative unmasking to generate regulatory DNA sequences. Following genus-specific fine-tuning on genome-derived intergenic sequences, DAPE-PD generated sequences that retained genus-associated compositional features despite low similarity to the fine-tuning datasets. Experimental validation identified functional de novo promoters, while in silico prioritization recovered active designs from small experimental candidate sets across three non-model gut commensals. candidates.title: AI-Powered Clinical Decision Support Tools
candidates.content: To the Editor The Viewpoint article by Drs Singh and Mello provides a balanced discussion of advertising in artificial intelligence (AI)–powered clinical decision support (CDS). It is worth highlighting that the authors state that AI-powered CDS often is free. Did we not say the same about drug company–sponsored lunches and so-called “free” pens and other giveaways in the 1990s? Some will recall when drug companies sponsored lunches for faculty and trainees, gave away pens and other branded items, and sometimes accompanied physicians on rounds. For those who trained more recently, please know that this practice was widely accepted; however, we eventually learned that there is, in fact, no free lunch. Now, we must learn there is no free CDS. Singh and Mello note that while “some products operate on a subscription model, others such as OpenEvidence use advertising revenue to offer access without charge.” It is surprising and disappointing that clinicians may think they are receiving CDS for free. Perhaps they have forgotten—or may have never learned—that drug company advertisements influence prescribing behavior when they appear alongside information intended to educate physicians an

candidates.title: AI-Powered Clinical Decision Support Tools—Reply
candidates.content: In Reply We appreciate the thoughtful letters in response to our Viewpoint. We agree with Dr Ziegelstein that the simplest solution to the ethical quandaries of advertising in AI-powered CDS tools would be for the AI-powered CDS companies that use advertisements and/or the pharmaceutical companies that partner with them to end this practice altogether. However, this is unlikely to happen, given that advertising is a potentially more lucrative revenue source than other options such as subscriptions. Ziegelstein’s suggestion that clinicians recognize they have other options and choose CDS tools that do not embed advertisements seems more realistic, particularly if their organizational employers nudge them in this direction. Historically, once Epocrates (a free drug information app) began supporting ads at the point of care, its credibility with its physician users eroded and other services such as UpToDate ultimately won out.

candidates.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Fecal Immunochemical Testing—Reply
candidates.content: In Reply We thank Dr Huynh and colleagues for their thoughtful comments on our economic evaluation of HPSA-FIT co-testing. Rather than modeling a program developed de novo, we evaluated the incremental value of integrating HPSA testing into an established colorectal cancer screening program. Accordingly, infrastructure development costs were not included in our analysis; however, this should not be interpreted as suggesting implementation requires only minimal investment. Health system readiness varies considerably across countries, but we regard such heterogeneity as support for a staged implementation strategy rather than a limitation: countries with established FIT programs can readily add HPSA testing to existing stool-based testing pathways, whereas those with less mature systems may need to strengthen registries, laboratory networks, referral pathways, and treatment capacity.

candidates.title: Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision?
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.33029v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Self-improving agents write lessons from the outcomes of their runs; when outcomes are noisy, a lesson can carry chance into later decisions. We measure one link of this chain in a registered study. In 256 synthetic worlds, each a recurring task with two interchangeable tools of recorded reliability, a scripted previous run used the more reliable tool (a good decision) or the less reliable one (a bad decision), with an assigned outcome: success or a transient failure. A model wrote a lesson from the run with ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction; a fresh session of the same model, holding the authoritative log and the previous result, chose the next run's first tool with one memory item: that lesson, the lesson from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive. The protocol was frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call; 11 LLM endpoints gave 90,084 answers. candidates.title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.35782v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cybersecurity governance, risk management, compliance, and security architecture rely on numerous concepts, including security properties, domains, controls, risks, implementation measures, capabilities, and compliance requirements. Although these concepts are widely used, they are often represented through heterogeneous abstractions and vocabularies, making relationships among them difficult to express consistently and leaving much of the associated reasoning dependent on expert knowledge. This paper introduces the concepts of Security Concerns and Atomic Security Concerns (ASCs) and explores the hypothesis that cybersecurity knowledge may be represented through a finite set of foundational concerns. Inspired by the role of atoms in chemistry, the proposed approach views cybersecurity concepts as compositions of more fundamental concerns rather than as independent abstractions. Hence, Atomic Security Concerns could be viewed as a common abstraction layer for the representation of cybersecurity concepts, independently of their domain, nature, or level of granularity. candidates.title: Recovering Business Rules as Cascade Lookups for Enterprise Field Prediction
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.34258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Enterprise sales-order systems rely on manually maintained configuration rules to determine fields such as payment terms, shipping points, and sales ownership. When these rules are incomplete or stale, operators must enter values by hand, and downstream errors spread into billing, logistics, and reporting. This paper studies whether missing or outdated rules can be recovered from historical transactions instead of being relearned as opaque statistical patterns. We introduce a knowledge-graph-guided workflow in which an LLM agent proposes candidate business keys, meaning column combinations such as customer and document type, validates them through SQL profiling, and compiles the resulting evidence into deterministic cascade lookups. The LLM is used only during offline rule discovery. At inference time, prediction is a transparent key lookup with no model-serving requirement. candidates.title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.35509v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large organizations consume large language models (LLMs) from several vendors at once, each with its own API dialect, credential model, streaming protocol and pricing. Integrated directly, this heterogeneity yields credential sprawl, format lock-in, unbounded spend and inconsistent governance. We present the design and production operation of the Cosmos LLM Gateway, the governed entry point for enterprise LLM traffic at PayPal. Built on Envoy, it splits work by latency profile: I/O-bound control decisions (authentication, credential brokering, policy and budget evaluation) run in an out-of-process external-processing service, while wire-format translation, token metering and prompt-cache shaping run in-proxy as a Rust WebAssembly filter, so that, by default, streamed response body chunks never wait on an out-of-process call. Models, providers and prices are largely validated data rather than code. Governance is declarative policy evaluated by Open Policy Agent and managed through a control plane with role-scoped authoring, approvals, pilots, shadow-mode rollout, usage notifications and versioned policy bundles. candidates.title: Measurement Without Validity: The Compounding Reliability Problem in Agentic AI Evaluation
candidates.content: arXiv:2608.00794v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic AI evaluation pipelines produce benchmark scores that justify deployment decisions, safety certifications, and regulatory compliance claims. No formal framework has characterized how validity degrades across these stages. We present a knowledge-based three-layer compounding validity model, $V_{\rm total} \leq V_1 \times V_2 \times V_3$, that captures multiplicative degradation across task generation ($V_1$), human-simulator calibration ($V_2$), and automated judgment ($V_3$). Applying it to five widely-used agentic benchmark configurations, we find $V_1$ and $V_2$ independently measurable and both degraded, but $V_3$ not currently quantifiable for any: three of the four benchmarks score with a single deterministic rule, so no second rater exists and reliability is undefined, and the fourth's partial LLM grader has no published grader-vs-human measurement.
